about: LL108 Criminal Law is a compulsory one-unit course on the LSE LLB in Laws (also on the BA in Anthropology and Law, and open to some other students). The 2026/27 course guide describes it as studying the general part of criminal law and selected offences, in the context of theories about the aims and functions of criminalisation: limits to criminalisation; the framework of liability (conduct, responsibility, capacity, defences); homicide; non-fatal violence; sexual offences; property offences; secondary participation; inchoate offences; and strict liability. Teaching in 2026/27 is lectures and classes across Autumn and Winter Terms, with at least two formative pieces (usually an essay and a problem question). Assessment is a single 180-minute exam (plus 15 minutes' reading time) in the Spring exam period, worth 100%. This pack states the law of England and Wales as at October 2026.
topics: Framework of liability: conduct, responsibility and capacity
Homicide: murder and the partial defences

notes.body:
The 2026/27 course guide for LL108 says the course studies criminal law "in the context of theories about the aims and functions of criminalisation", and the first topic asks what should be a crime at all. Expect essay questions that test doctrine against these theories.

Why criminal law is special
- Conviction brings state punishment and public censure, so it needs stronger justification than civil liability.
- The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt (Woolmington v DPP [1935] AC 462), and Article 6(2) ECHR protects the presumption of innocence.
- Article 7 ECHR (no punishment without law) requires offences to be defined clearly enough for people to foresee liability.

The harm principle
- John Stuart Mill, On Liberty (1859): the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others. Harm to oneself is not enough.
- Joel Feinberg, The Moral Limits of the Criminal Law (four volumes, 1984 to 1988), develops the harm principle and adds an "offence principle" for serious offence to others.
- Problem: "harm" is elastic. Almost any conduct can be described as harmful to someone, so the principle may not limit much in practice.

Legal moralism: the Hart–Devlin debate
- The Wolfenden Report (1957) recommended decriminalising private homosexual acts between consenting adults, on the basis that some private morality is "not the law's business". The Sexual Offences Act 1967 partly implemented this for England and Wales.
- Patrick Devlin (Maccabaean Lecture 1959, published in The Enforcement of Morals, 1965) argued that society may use law to protect its shared morality, since that morality holds society together.
- H L A Hart, Law, Liberty and Morality (1963), replied that there is no evidence that deviation from shared morality threatens society, and distinguished paternalism (which he accepted in some cases) from enforcing morality as such.
- Shaw v DPP [1962] AC 220 (conspiracy to corrupt public morals) is the classic example of judges enforcing morality.

Paternalism and consent
R v Brown [1994] 1 AC 212 upheld convictions for consensual sado-masochistic injuries. The majority stressed public interest and risk; the dissents (Lords Mustill and Slynn) treated it as private conduct. The case is a standard test for the harm principle (see the non-fatal violence topic).

Minimalism and overcriminalisation
- Writers such as Douglas Husak (Overcriminalization, 2008) and Andrew Ashworth argue that the criminal law is used too readily, especially through large numbers of regulatory and strict liability offences.
- Principles proposed to limit criminalisation include: last resort (use civil or regulatory tools first), proportionality, and fair labelling (the offence name should reflect the wrong).
- Nicola Lacey and others writing in a critical tradition (Reconstructing Criminal Law is one of the course textbooks) ask how criminalisation reflects social and political choices, not just abstract principle.

Recent examples to test theories
- Decriminalisation: the Crime and Policing Act 2026, Part 16 (s 241), removes women from the criminal law relating to abortion of their own pregnancies in England and Wales; the general law on abortion by others is otherwise kept. Section 241 came into force on Royal Assent (29 April 2026).
- New offences: the same Act creates many offences (e.g. assaulting a retail worker, s 45, and a specific spiking offence, s 134). These come into force only on a day set by regulations (s 255(1)); they were not among the provisions commenced on 29 June 2026, and in July 2026 the Government had not set a date, so check legislation.gov.uk before treating them as in force.

Exam tips: in essays, set out a theory (Mill, Devlin, Hart, Feinberg), apply it to a concrete offence or case, and reach a view on whether the law can be justified.

The 2026/27 course guide describes this part of the course as the conceptual framework of criminal liability: conduct, responsibility, capacity and defences. This note covers the building blocks; defences are in the next topic.

Actus reus
The actus reus covers the external elements of an offence: conduct, circumstances and (for result crimes) consequences.
- Voluntariness: conduct must be voluntary. Hill v Baxter [1958] 1 QB 277 gives examples of involuntary acts, such as being attacked by a swarm of bees while driving.
- Omissions: there is no general duty to act, but liability for failing to act arises where there is a duty, for example:
  - under a contract (R v Pittwood (1902) 19 TLR 37, level-crossing keeper);
  - from a family relationship (R v Gibbins and Proctor (1918) 13 Cr App R 134);
  - from voluntarily assuming care of a dependent person (R v Stone and Dobinson [1977] QB 354);
  - from creating a dangerous situation (R v Miller [1983] 2 AC 161, cigarette fire; R v Evans [2009] EWCA Crim 650, supplying drugs).
- Withdrawing life support from a patient in a persistent vegetative state was treated as an omission in Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789.

Causation (for result crimes)
- Factual: "but for" D's conduct, would the result have occurred? (R v White [1910] 2 KB 124: poison did not cause death, so attempted murder only.)
- Legal: D's conduct must be an operating and substantial (more than minimal) cause (R v Smith [1959] 2 QB 35).
- Medical treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent of D's acts and so potent that D's contribution becomes insignificant (R v Cheshire [1991] 1 WLR 844).
- A reasonably foreseeable reaction by the victim, such as escaping, does not break the chain unless it is "daft" (R v Roberts (1971) 56 Cr App R 95).
- Take your victim as you find them (R v Blaue [1975] 1 WLR 1411: refusal of a blood transfusion on religious grounds).
- A free, deliberate and informed act of an adult (e.g. self-injecting drugs) breaks the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] UKHL 38).

Mens rea
- Intention: direct (aim or purpose) or oblique, where the result is a virtual certainty and D appreciates this (R v Woollin [1999] 1 AC 82; see the murder topic).
- Recklessness is subjective: D is reckless as to a result if aware of a risk that it will occur and it is unreasonable to take that risk (R v G [2003] UKHL 50, overruling Caldwell). R v Cunningham [1957] 2 QB 396 is the earlier subjective test.
- Negligence is an objective standard, used for gross negligence manslaughter and some statutory offences.
- Coincidence of actus reus and mens rea: a continuing act (Fagan v MPC [1969] 1 QB 439) or a series of acts (Thabo Meli v R [1954] 1 WLR 228) can satisfy it.
- Transferred malice: intent to harm one victim transfers to another actually harmed (R v Latimer (1886) 17 QBD 359), but not between different kinds of offence (R v Pembliton (1874)).

Capacity
- The age of criminal responsibility in England and Wales is 10 (Children and Young Persons Act 1933, s 50). The old presumption that children aged 10 to 13 were incapable of crime (doli incapax) was abolished by the Crime and Disorder Act 1998, s 34, and the House of Lords held in R v JTB [2009] UKHL 20 that the defence went with it.
- Companies: traditionally liable only through the "directing mind and will" (Tesco Supermarkets v Nattrass [1972] AC 153). The Crime and Policing Act 2026, s 250, now makes an organisation liable for any offence committed by a senior manager acting within the actual or apparent scope of their authority. It came into force on 29 June 2026 (two months after Royal Assent, under s 255(3)) and replaces the narrower rule for economic crimes in s 196 of the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023.

Exam tips: for every offence, set out actus reus, causation (if a result crime), mens rea and coincidence, before looking at defences.

Defences are usually classed as justifications (the conduct was right or permissible, e.g. self-defence) or excuses (the conduct was wrong but D is not blameworthy, e.g. duress). The distinction matters in theory essays about responsibility.

Self-defence and prevention of crime
The common law defence and s 3 of the Criminal Law Act 1967 are explained by the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s 76:
- D is judged on the facts as D honestly believed them to be, even if the mistake was unreasonable (s 76(3)–(4); R v Williams (Gladstone) (1984) 78 Cr App R 276; Beckford v R [1988] AC 130).
- But D cannot rely on a mistake caused by voluntary intoxication (s 76(5)).
- The force used must be objectively reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them. Disproportionate force is never reasonable (s 76(6)), except that in a "householder case" force is unreasonable only if grossly disproportionate (s 76(5A)). R (Collins) v Secretary of State for Justice [2016] EWHC 33 (Admin) held that force which is disproportionate but not grossly so must still be reasonable in all the circumstances.
- No duty to retreat, but the chance to retreat is a factor (s 76(6A)). A person acting in the heat of the moment cannot weigh force to a nicety (s 76(7)).

Duress by threats and of circumstances
- Test (R v Graham [1982] 1 WLR 294, approved in R v Howe [1987] AC 417): was D compelled to act because D reasonably believed there was a threat of death or serious injury, and would a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing D's characteristics have responded in the same way?
- R v Hasan [2005] UKHL 22: there is little room for the defence unless D reasonably expected the threatened harm to follow immediately or almost immediately, so that no evasive action was reasonably possible; D cannot rely on duress if D voluntarily associated with people D foresaw or ought reasonably to have foreseen might subject D to compulsion by threats of violence.
- Not available to murder (Howe) or attempted murder (R v Gotts [1992] 2 AC 412).
- Duress of circumstances applies the same test where the danger comes from a situation rather than a person's demand (R v Conway [1989] QB 290; R v Martin [1989] 1 All ER 652).

Necessity
- R v Dudley and Stephens (1884) 14 QBD 273: necessity is no defence to murder (shipwrecked sailors who killed and ate a cabin boy).
- Re A (Children) (Conjoined Twins: Surgical Separation) [2001] Fam 147: separating conjoined twins, which would kill the weaker twin, was lawful in the exceptional circumstances.

Insanity and automatism
- Insanity (M'Naghten's Case (1843) 10 Cl & F 200): a defect of reason, from a disease of the mind, so that D did not know the nature and quality of the act or did not know it was wrong. "Wrong" means legally wrong (R v Windle [1952] 2 QB 826; R v Johnson [2007] EWCA Crim 1978). D must prove insanity on the balance of probabilities. The verdict is not guilty by reason of insanity, with flexible disposal.
- "Disease of the mind" is a legal concept based on an internal cause: epilepsy (R v Sullivan [1984] AC 156), diabetic hyperglycaemia (R v Hennessy [1989] 1 WLR 287) and sleepwalking (R v Burgess [1991] 2 QB 92) have all been treated as insanity.
- Non-insane automatism needs an external cause and leads to a complete acquittal: hypoglycaemia caused by taking insulin (R v Quick [1973] QB 910).

Intoxication
- Voluntary intoxication can negate a specific intent (e.g. intent to kill for murder) but is no defence to crimes of basic intent where recklessness suffices (DPP v Majewski [1977] AC 443).
- Involuntary intoxication is no defence if D still formed the mens rea (R v Kingston [1995] 2 AC 355).

Exam tips: check whether the defence is complete or partial, who bears the burden (the prosecution must disprove most defences once raised; D must prove insanity), and whether the defence is excluded for the offence charged.

Murder is the unlawful killing of a human being under the King's peace with malice aforethought. It carries a mandatory life sentence, which shapes much of the law, including the partial defences that reduce murder to manslaughter.

The actus reus
- D must cause the death of a human being (born alive and not yet dead). The year-and-a-day rule was abolished by the Law Reform (Year and a Day Rule) Act 1996.
- Causation follows the general rules (see the conduct and responsibility topic).

Malice aforethought
- Intention to kill or to cause grievous bodily harm (R v Vickers [1957] 2 QB 664; R v Cunningham [1982] AC 566). GBH means "really serious harm" (DPP v Smith [1961] AC 290).
- Because intent to cause serious harm is enough, a person can be convicted of murder without intending or foreseeing death. Critics say this is unfair labelling.

Oblique intention
- R v Moloney [1985] AC 905 and R v Hancock and Shankland [1986] AC 455 held that foresight of consequences is evidence of intention, not intention itself.
- R v Woollin [1999] 1 AC 82: the jury is not entitled to find the necessary intention unless death or serious bodily harm was a virtual certainty (barring some unforeseen intervention) as a result of D's actions, and D appreciated that was the case.
- R v Matthews and Alleyne [2003] EWCA Crim 192: Woollin states a rule of evidence; foresight of virtual certainty allows, but does not compel, a finding of intention.

Diminished responsibility (Homicide Act 1957, s 2, as substituted by the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, s 52)
D must prove, on the balance of probabilities, an abnormality of mental functioning which:
- arose from a recognised medical condition;
- substantially impaired D's ability to understand the nature of the conduct, form a rational judgment, or exercise self-control; and
- provides an explanation for the killing, meaning it caused or was a significant contributory factor in causing it.
In R v Golds [2016] UKSC 61 the Supreme Court held that "substantially" means important or weighty, not just more than trivial; judges should not normally define the word for the jury.

Loss of control (Coroners and Justice Act 2009, ss 54–56)
This replaced provocation (abolished by s 56). It needs:
- a loss of self-control, which need not be sudden (s 54(2)), and not a considered desire for revenge (s 54(4));
- a qualifying trigger (s 55): fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person, or things done or said which were circumstances of an extremely grave character and caused D a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged, or both;
- that a person of D's sex and age, with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint and in D's circumstances, might have reacted in the same or a similar way (s 54(1)(c)).
Sexual infidelity is disregarded as a trigger (s 55(6)(c)), but R v Clinton [2012] EWCA Crim 2 held it can be considered as context where it is integral to the facts. A trigger D incited as an excuse for violence does not count (s 55(6)(a)–(b)). D bears only an evidential burden; the prosecution must then disprove the defence (s 54(5)–(6)).

Reform
In June 2026 the Law Commission published a consultation paper on homicide offences (consultation open 17 June to 30 September 2026). It provisionally proposes three tiers: first-degree murder (killing with intent to kill, mandatory life sentence), second-degree murder (killing with intent to cause serious injury, maximum of life but not mandatory) and manslaughter. It also proposes a new verdict of "murder with a partial defence" (discretionary maximum of life) where D intended to kill but a partial defence such as loss of control applies, instead of a manslaughter verdict. Partial defences and murder sentencing are left to a further consultation paper expected in summer 2027, so check for developments.

Exam tips: in problem questions, establish murder first (causation, intent with Woollin if needed), then consider diminished responsibility and loss of control separately.

Involuntary manslaughter covers unlawful killings without malice aforethought. Sentencing is discretionary, up to life. There are two main forms in England and Wales: unlawful act (constructive) manslaughter and gross negligence manslaughter. Reckless manslaughter is sometimes recognised as a third form.

Unlawful act manslaughter
The prosecution must prove:
- an unlawful act: a criminal offence (not just a civil wrong), with its own mens rea. In R v Lamb [1967] 2 QB 981 there was no assault, because the victim did not apprehend violence and Lamb did not intend it, so no unlawful act.
- the act must be an act, not an omission (the omission cases go to gross negligence).
- dangerousness: the act must be such that all sober and reasonable people would inevitably recognise it must subject the victim to the risk of some harm, albeit not serious harm (R v Church [1966] 1 QB 59). D need not personally foresee harm (DPP v Newbury and Jones [1977] AC 500, paving stone thrown from a bridge).
- the reasonable person has the knowledge D had or would have gained during the act. In R v Watson [1989] 1 WLR 684 a burglar who saw during the burglary that the occupier was a frail 87-year-old was treated as aware of that (the conviction was quashed on causation grounds). In R v Dawson (1985) 81 Cr App R 150, a heart attack after an attempted robbery was not enough because a reasonable person would not have known of the victim's heart condition. Harm means physical harm, which can include shock that causes physical injury.
- the act must cause death. In drug-supply cases, the victim's free, deliberate and informed decision to self-inject breaks the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2) [2007] UKHL 38).

Gross negligence manslaughter
Following R v Adomako [1995] 1 AC 171, restated in R v Broughton [2020] EWCA Crim 1093:
- D owed V a duty of care (using ordinary negligence principles; e.g. doctor and patient, employer and worker, or the duty situations for omissions);
- D breached it;
- at the time of breach there was a serious and obvious risk of death (not just serious injury) that was reasonably foreseeable to a reasonable person in D's position (R v Misra and Srivastava [2004] EWCA Crim 2375; R v Rose [2017] EWCA Crim 1168);
- the breach caused death;
- the breach was so bad, in all the circumstances, that it should be judged criminal: "gross" negligence is for the jury.
In Rose an optometrist who failed to examine the back of a child's eyes was acquitted on appeal: the risk of death must be foreseeable on what D actually knew at the time, not on what a proper examination would have revealed. Misra held that the test is not too vague to satisfy Article 7 ECHR.

Reckless manslaughter
Where D foresees a risk of death or serious injury and unjustifiably takes it, but lacks malice aforethought, the killing can be manslaughter. It is rarely charged separately.

Corporate manslaughter
Under the Corporate Manslaughter and Corporate Homicide Act 2007, an organisation is guilty if the way its activities are managed or organised causes a death and amounts to a gross breach of a relevant duty of care, and the way senior management organised them is a substantial element in the breach.

Critique and reform
- Unlawful act manslaughter is criticised as constructive liability: a minor assault that unexpectedly kills is labelled homicide.
- The Law Commission's June 2026 homicide consultation paper provisionally proposes manslaughter as the third tier below two degrees of murder, with reformed versions of reckless, unlawful act and gross negligence manslaughter.

Exam tips: always ask first whether there was a criminal unlawful act with mens rea; if the killing arose from an omission or a lawful activity done badly, switch to gross negligence.

The main offences are in the Criminal Justice Act 1988 and the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 (OAPA). They form a ladder of seriousness, though critics note that the 1861 wording is outdated and the ladder is uneven.

Common assault and battery (Criminal Justice Act 1988, s 39; summary only, maximum 6 months)
- Assault: causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force. Words alone (R v Constanza [1997] 2 Cr App R 492, letters) and even silent phone calls (R v Ireland; R v Burstow [1998] AC 147) can suffice. Words can also negate an assault (Tuberville v Savage (1669)).
- Battery: the application of unlawful force, however slight. Touching beyond what is generally acceptable in ordinary life is a battery (Collins v Willcock [1984] 1 WLR 1172). It can be indirect (Haystead v Chief Constable of Derbyshire [2000] 3 All ER 890).
- Mens rea: intention or subjective recklessness as to causing apprehension or applying force (R v Venna [1976] QB 421; R v Savage; DPP v Parmenter [1992] 1 AC 699).

Assault occasioning actual bodily harm (OAPA s 47; maximum 5 years)
- ABH is any hurt or injury interfering with health or comfort that is more than transient or trifling. It includes psychiatric injury but not mere emotions (R v Chan-Fook [1994] 1 WLR 689), cutting off a substantial amount of hair (DPP v Smith (Michael) [2006] EWHC 94 (Admin)) and brief loss of consciousness (T v DPP [2003] EWHC 266 (Admin)).
- "Occasioning" is causation; a victim's reasonable escape does not break the chain (R v Roberts (1971)).
- Mens rea: only that for the assault or battery. No foresight of harm is needed (Savage).

Wounding or inflicting GBH (OAPA s 20; maximum 5 years)
- Wound: a break in both layers of the skin (JCC (a minor) v Eisenhower [1984] QB 331).
- GBH: really serious harm (DPP v Smith [1961]), judged in light of the victim's age and health (R v Bollom [2003] EWCA Crim 2846). It includes serious psychiatric injury (Burstow).
- "Inflict" does not require an assault (Burstow).
- Mens rea: "maliciously" means D foresaw that some physical harm, though not necessarily serious harm, might result (R v Mowatt [1968] 1 QB 421; Parmenter).

Wounding or causing GBH with intent (OAPA s 18; maximum life)
- Intent to cause GBH (or to resist or prevent arrest). Recklessness is not enough (R v Belfon [1976] 1 WLR 741).

Consent
- Consent is a defence to assault and battery but generally not where ABH or more is intended or caused (Attorney-General's Reference (No 6 of 1980) [1981] QB 715; R v Brown [1994] 1 AC 212), unless an exception applies: properly conducted sport (R v Barnes [2004] EWCA Crim 3246), surgery, tattooing, rough horseplay, and consensual marital branding in R v Wilson [1997] QB 47.
- Body modification is not an exception (R v BM [2018] EWCA Crim 560).
- Consent to the risk of sexually transmitted infection can be a defence to s 20, but only if informed (R v Dica [2004] EWCA Crim 1103; R v Konzani [2005] EWCA Crim 706).
- Domestic Abuse Act 2021, s 71: consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is no defence (putting R v Brown on a statutory footing).

Newer offences
- Intentional strangulation or suffocation (Serious Crime Act 2015, s 75A, inserted by the Domestic Abuse Act 2021).
- The Crime and Policing Act 2026 creates offences of assaulting a retail worker (s 45) and administering a harmful substance, including by spiking (s 134). Both come into force only on a day set by regulations; neither was commenced on 29 June 2026, so check legislation.gov.uk before treating them as in force.

Exam tips: identify the harm first (none, ABH, wound or GBH), choose the matching offence, then check mens rea carefully, because s 47 and s 20 need no foresight of the harm actually caused.

The core offences are in the Sexual Offences Act 2003 (SOA), which applies in England and Wales. Most problem questions turn on consent.

The main offences
- Rape (s 1): A intentionally penetrates the vagina, anus or mouth of B with his penis; B does not consent; and A does not reasonably believe that B consents. Maximum life.
- Assault by penetration (s 2): penetration with a part of the body or anything else, sexual, without consent or reasonable belief.
- Sexual assault (s 3): intentional sexual touching without consent or reasonable belief.
- Causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent (s 4).
- Whether A's belief is reasonable is decided having regard to all the circumstances, including any steps A took to find out whether B consents (s 1(2)).

The meaning of consent (s 74)
A person consents if they agree by choice and have the freedom and capacity to make that choice.
- Capacity and intoxication: a drunken consent is still consent if the complainant retains capacity; capacity can be lost through drink before unconsciousness (R v Bree [2007] EWCA Crim 804).
- Conditional consent: consent given on a condition about how the act is done may be negated if the condition is broken. Examples are a condition that a condom is used (Assange v Swedish Prosecution Authority [2011] EWHC 2849 (Admin)) or that the man withdraws before ejaculation (R (F) v DPP [2013] EWHC 945 (Admin)).
- Deception: in R v McNally [2013] EWCA Crim 1051 deception about gender negated consent. But in R v Lawrance [2020] EWCA Crim 971 a lie about having had a vasectomy did not, because it was about the consequences of the act rather than its physical performance.
- Non-disclosure of HIV status does not of itself negate consent to intercourse for rape (R v B [2006] EWCA Crim 2945), though it may found a s 20 offence (see the non-fatal violence topic).

The evidential presumptions (s 75)
If A did the act and knew certain circumstances existed, B is presumed not to consent and A not to have reasonably believed in consent unless sufficient evidence is raised to the contrary. The circumstances include violence or fear of immediate violence against B or another, B being unlawfully detained, B being asleep or unconscious, B being unable to communicate consent because of physical disability, and B having been given a substance capable of stupefying or overpowering B without consent.

The conclusive presumptions (s 76)
Lack of consent and lack of reasonable belief are conclusively presumed where A intentionally deceived B as to the nature or purpose of the act, or induced B to consent by impersonating someone known personally to B. Courts read s 76 narrowly because it removes any defence (R v Jheeta [2007] EWCA Crim 1699); most deceptions are dealt with under s 74.

Children
Offences such as rape of a child under 13 (s 5) are committed whatever the defendant believed about age or consent. R v G [2008] UKHL 37 held that this strict liability as to age does not breach Article 6 ECHR.

Recent law
The Crime and Policing Act 2026, Part 5, creates and amends a range of sexual offences, for example on child sexual abuse image-generators (s 72) and intimate images (s 98). Some Part 5 provisions came into force on 29 June 2026 and others still await commencement regulations, so check each one before relying on it.

Critique
Debates include: whether the s 74 definition gives clear guidance; which deceptions should negate consent (compare McNally with Lawrance); how far s 1(2) protects against unreasonable beliefs; and the low conviction rate for rape.

Exam tips: work through s 76, then s 75, then s 74; deal with consent and reasonable belief separately.

The main offences are in the Theft Act 1968 and the Fraud Act 2006.

Theft (Theft Act 1968, s 1; maximum 7 years)
A person is guilty of theft if he dishonestly appropriates property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it.
- Appropriation (s 3): any assumption of the rights of an owner. Assuming any one right is enough (R v Morris [1984] AC 320). It does not matter that the owner consented (Lawrence v MPC [1972] AC 626; R v Gomez [1993] AC 442), and even receiving a valid gift can be an appropriation (R v Hinks [2001] 2 AC 241), leaving dishonesty to do the work.
- Property (s 4): includes money, real and personal property, and things in action; land, wild plants and wild creatures only in limited cases. Confidential information is not property (Oxford v Moss (1979) 68 Cr App R 183).
- Belonging to another (s 5): anyone with possession, control or a proprietary interest, so an owner can steal his own car from a garage in possession of it (R v Turner (No 2) [1971] 1 WLR 901). See also s 5(3) (obligation to deal with property in a particular way) and s 5(4) (property got by another's mistake: Attorney-General's Reference (No 1 of 1983) [1985] QB 182, overpaid wages).
- Intention to permanently deprive (s 6): includes treating the thing as one's own to dispose of regardless of the owner's rights, and borrowing for a period and in circumstances equivalent to an outright taking. Taking films to copy and returning them undamaged was not enough in R v Lloyd [1985] QB 829, because their "goodness and virtue" were not gone.

Dishonesty
- Section 2(1): D is not dishonest if D believes he has a legal right to the property, believes the owner would consent, or (unless a trustee or personal representative) believes the owner cannot be found by reasonable steps.
- Otherwise apply Ivey v Genting Casinos [2017] UKSC 67, confirmed for criminal cases in R v Barton and Booth [2020] EWCA Crim 575: (1) what was D's actual knowledge or belief as to the facts? (2) was D's conduct dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people? The old second question in R v Ghosh [1982] QB 1053 (did D realise ordinary people would think it dishonest?) no longer applies.

Robbery (s 8; maximum life)
Stealing, and immediately before or at the time of doing so, and in order to do so, using force on any person or putting or seeking to put any person in fear of force.
- No theft, no robbery: a genuine belief in a legal right negates dishonesty (R v Robinson [1977] Crim LR 173).
- Little force is needed: a nudge can be enough (R v Dawson and James (1976) 64 Cr App R 170).
- Appropriation can be a continuing act (R v Hale (1979) 68 Cr App R 415).

Burglary (s 9; maximum 14 years for a dwelling, 10 otherwise)
- s 9(1)(a): entering a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to steal, inflict GBH or do unlawful damage.
- s 9(1)(b): having entered as a trespasser, stealing or attempting to steal, or inflicting or attempting to inflict GBH.
- Entry must be "effective" (R v Brown [1985] Crim LR 212); a man stuck halfway through a window had entered (R v Ryan (1996) 160 JP 610).
- Exceeding permission makes D a trespasser (R v Jones and Smith [1976] 1 WLR 672); going behind a shop counter can be entering a part of a building as a trespasser (R v Walkington [1979] 1 WLR 1169).

Fraud (Fraud Act 2006; maximum 10 years)
Fraud can be committed by false representation (s 2), failing to disclose information under a legal duty (s 3) or abuse of position (s 4), each done dishonestly with intent to make a gain or cause a loss. No one need actually be deceived or lose anything.

Recent change: the Crime and Policing Act 2026, s 47, makes shop theft triable either way whatever the value of the goods (removing the £200 low-value rule). It comes into force only on a day set by regulations and was not commenced on 29 June 2026, so check legislation.gov.uk before treating it as in force.

Exam tips: take each element of theft in turn, then build up to robbery or burglary; always apply s 2 before the Ivey test.

Secondary parties (accessories) are liable for the offence committed by the principal. Under the Accessories and Abettors Act 1861, s 8, anyone who aids, abets, counsels or procures an indictable offence is liable to be tried and punished as a principal (for summary offences, see the Magistrates' Courts Act 1980, s 44).

Conduct element
- Aiding: giving help, before or during the offence.
- Abetting and counselling: encouraging, usually at the scene (abetting) or beforehand (counselling). For counselling there must be contact and the principal must act within the scope of the encouragement, but no strict causal link is needed (R v Calhaem [1985] QB 808).
- Procuring: bringing about the offence. It needs causation but no meeting of minds, as where D secretly spiked a driver's drink (Attorney-General's Reference (No 1 of 1975) [1975] QB 773).
- Mere presence is not enough (R v Coney (1882) 8 QBD 534; R v Clarkson [1971] 1 WLR 1402), but presence intended to encourage and actually encouraging can be (Wilcox v Jeffery [1951] 1 All ER 464, a jazz critic who attended an illegal performance).
- Failing to use a right of control can be aiding (Du Cros v Lambourne [1907] 1 KB 40, a car owner).

Mental element after Jogee
R v Jogee; Ruddock v The Queen [2016] UKSC 8 held that the law had taken a wrong turn in Chan Wing-Siu v R [1985] AC 168 and R v Powell; R v English [1999] 1 AC 1, which had made foresight that the principal might commit a further crime enough.
- D must intend to assist or encourage the principal to commit the crime. This includes knowledge of any existing facts necessary for the principal's conduct to be criminal (see Johnson v Youden [1950] 1 KB 544; National Coal Board v Gamble [1959] 1 QB 11).
- Intention to assist is not the same as desire: D may hope the crime will not happen.
- Conditional intent is enough: if D joins a plan to rob on the basis that violence will be used if necessary, D intends to assist that violence.
- Foresight is evidence, sometimes strong evidence, of intent, but it is not intent.
- Where D intends to assist a crime of violence and the principal kills, D is guilty of murder only if D intended to assist intentional killing or intentional infliction of serious harm. If D lacked that intent but took part in an unlawful act that a reasonable person would realise carried a risk of some harm, and death resulted, D is guilty of manslaughter.
- Jogee also recognised that an "overwhelming supervening event" by the principal, which no one in D's position could have contemplated, can break the link.
- Convictions under the old law are not automatically unsafe: appeals out of time require "substantial injustice" (R v Johnson [2016] EWCA Crim 1613).

Withdrawal
- In pre-planned crimes, withdrawal requires more than a change of heart or simply leaving. There usually must be timely and unequivocal communication of withdrawal to the others (R v Becerra and Cooper (1975) 62 Cr App R 212; R v Rook [1993] 1 WLR 1005), and the closer the crime is, the more may be required.
- In spontaneous violence, communication is not essential; walking away may be enough (R v Mitchell and King (1999) 163 JP 75). Whether D has done enough to withdraw is a question of fact and degree for the jury (R v O'Flaherty [2004] EWCA Crim 526).

Other rules
- The victim rule: a person whom an offence exists to protect cannot be an accessory to it (R v Tyrrell [1894] 1 QB 710).
- An accessory can be liable even if the principal is acquitted, where the actus reus was committed (R v Cogan and Leak [1976] QB 217).
- Gnango [2011] UKSC 59: D, who agreed to a shoot-out, was guilty of murder when the opponent's shot killed a passer-by.

Exam tips: identify the principal's offence, then the accessory's conduct, then intention post-Jogee (including conditional intent), then any withdrawal.

Inchoate offences (attempt, conspiracy, and encouraging or assisting crime) punish conduct before the intended crime is completed, raising the question of how early the law should intervene.

Attempt (Criminal Attempts Act 1981)
- Section 1(1): with intent to commit an offence, D does an act which is more than merely preparatory to the commission of the offence.
- Applies to offences triable on indictment, but not to conspiracy or aiding and abetting (s 1(4)).
- The maximum sentence is the same as for the full offence (s 4).

When is an act "more than merely preparatory"?
- The question is for the jury, once the judge decides there is evidence on which they could find it (s 4(3)).
- D must have "embarked on the crime proper" (R v Gullefer [1990] 1 WLR 1063), though D need not have reached the last act or "point of no return".
- R v Jones [1990] 1 WLR 1057: getting into V's car and pointing a loaded sawn-off shotgun at him was enough, even though the safety catch was on.
- R v Campbell (1991) 93 Cr App R 350: a man with an imitation gun near a post office, who had not entered, had not gone beyond preparation.
- R v Geddes [1996] Crim LR 894: a man found in school toilets with rope and a knife had not attempted false imprisonment; the question was whether he had actually tried to commit the offence.
- R v Tosti [1997] Crim LR 746: examining the padlock on a barn door with cutting equipment hidden nearby was an attempted burglary.

Mens rea of attempt
- Intention as to the consequences required by the full offence: attempted murder needs intent to kill, not just intent to cause GBH (R v Whybrow (1951) 35 Cr App R 141).
- As to circumstances, recklessness can be enough where it is enough for the full offence: attempted rape where D was reckless as to consent (R v Khan [1990] 1 WLR 813); and see Attorney-General's Reference (No 3 of 1992) (1994) 98 Cr App R 383.

Impossibility
- D can be guilty of attempting an offence that is impossible to commit (s 1(2)), judged on the facts as D believed them (s 1(3)).
- R v Shivpuri [1987] AC 1: a man who believed he was dealing in drugs, but had harmless vegetable matter, was guilty of attempt. The House of Lords overruled Anderton v Ryan [1985] AC 560, decided only about a year earlier, using the 1966 Practice Statement.

Conspiracy (Criminal Law Act 1977)
- Section 1(1): agreeing with another that a course of conduct will be pursued which, if carried out as intended, will necessarily amount to or involve an offence by one or more of the parties (or would do so but for impossibility).
- Where the offence requires knowledge of a circumstance, each conspirator must intend or know that the circumstance will exist at the time (s 1(2); R v Saik [2006] UKHL 18). Suspicion is not enough.
- No conspiracy if the only other party is one's spouse or civil partner, a child under the age of criminal responsibility, or the intended victim (s 2(2)).
- Common law conspiracy to defraud survives (Scott v Metropolitan Police Commissioner [1975] AC 819).

Encouraging or assisting crime (Serious Crime Act 2007, Part 2)
- s 44: doing an act capable of encouraging or assisting an offence, intending to encourage or assist its commission.
- s 45: doing such an act believing the offence will be committed and that the act will encourage or assist it.
- s 46: believing that one or more of a number of offences will be committed.
- The offence is complete even if no offence is ever committed; s 50 gives a defence of acting reasonably; s 59 abolished common law incitement.

Theory: subjectivists stress D's intention and support liability for impossible attempts; objectivists stress harm or danger and are uneasy about punishing conduct like Shivpuri's.

Exam tips: for attempt, deal with actus reus (more than merely preparatory, using the cases on proximity) and mens rea separately, and check impossibility if D was mistaken about the facts.

A strict liability offence is one where no mens rea is required for at least one element of the actus reus. Most are statutory regulatory offences (food safety, pollution, licensing, road traffic), but some are serious, such as the age element of child sex offences.

The presumption of mens rea
- Courts presume that Parliament intended mens rea to be required, even when the statute is silent (Sweet v Parsley [1970] AC 132: a teacher who sublet a farmhouse was not "concerned in the management" of premises used for smoking cannabis without knowledge).
- B (A Minor) v DPP [2000] 2 AC 428 and R v K [2001] UKHL 41: the presumption applied to the age element of the old offences of indecency with and indecent assault on a child, so an honest belief that the child was over the age was a defence.
- Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v Attorney-General of Hong Kong [1985] AC 1 (Lord Scarman): the presumption is particularly strong for "truly criminal" offences; it can be displaced only clearly or by necessary implication; the only situation in which it can be displaced is where the statute deals with an issue of social concern such as public safety; and even then strict liability must promote the statute's object by encouraging greater vigilance.

Examples where strict liability was found
- Cundy v Le Cocq (1884) 13 QBD 207: selling alcohol to a drunk person.
- Callow v Tillstone (1900) 83 LT 411: a butcher sold unfit meat even though a vet had certified it.
- Alphacell Ltd v Woodward [1972] AC 824: causing polluted matter to enter a river.
- Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Storkwain Ltd [1986] 1 WLR 903: supplying drugs on a forged prescription.
- Harrow LBC v Shah [2000] 1 WLR 83: selling a lottery ticket to an under-16.
- R v G [2008] UKHL 37: rape of a child under 13 (Sexual Offences Act 2003, s 5) is strict as to age; Article 6(2) ECHR concerns procedure and does not control the substantive elements of an offence.
- Contrast Sherras v De Rutzen [1895] 1 QB 918, where a publican who served an on-duty constable who had removed his armband was not guilty because knowledge was required.

Arguments for strict liability
- Protects the public in areas of social concern.
- Encourages high standards and vigilance by businesses.
- Makes enforcement practical: proving the mens rea of a company or busy trader is hard.
- Usually low penalties and little stigma.

Arguments against
- Punishes the morally blameless, breaking the link between liability and fault.
- There is little evidence it improves standards more than fault-based offences.
- Labels and penalties for some strict offences are serious (e.g. the child sex offences in R v G).
- Regulatory offences account for much of the growth in criminal law that overcriminalisation critics attack (see the limits to criminalisation topic).

Compromises
- Many statutes include a due diligence defence: D is not guilty if they took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence (for example the Food Safety Act 1990, s 21).
- Negligence-based liability is an intermediate option.

Exam tips: in problem questions, start from the presumption (Sweet v Parsley; B v DPP), apply the Gammon factors to the wording, subject matter and penalty, and then look for any statutory defence.

cards.b: The only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over anyone against their will is to prevent harm to others; harm to self is not enough (On Liberty).
Society may use criminal law to protect its shared morality, because that morality is part of what holds society together (Maccabaean Lecture 1959).
Law, Liberty and Morality (1963): no evidence that private immorality threatens society; paternalism can be justified but enforcing morality as such cannot.
Recommended decriminalising private homosexual acts between consenting adults; some private morality is not the law's business. Partly implemented by the Sexual Offences Act 1967.
Criminalisation may be justified to prevent serious offence (not just harm) to others, weighed against the value of the conduct and how easily it can be avoided.
The name and structure of an offence should reflect the nature and seriousness of the wrong, so conviction communicates accurately what the offender did.
The external elements of an offence: conduct, the circumstances in which it occurs, and (for result crimes) its consequences; conduct must be voluntary.

cards.f: Duty to act: Stone and Dobinson [1977]
cards.b: A duty arises where D voluntarily assumes care of a dependent person who cannot care for themselves; failure to act can then found manslaughter.
D who creates a dangerous situation (fire from a cigarette) and becomes aware of it has a duty to take reasonable steps to counteract it.
Negligent medical treatment breaks the chain of causation only if so independent and so potent that D's acts are insignificant.
Subjective: D is aware of a risk that a circumstance exists or result will occur, and it is unreasonable in the circumstances as known to D to take it.
D's mens rea towards one victim transfers to the actual victim of the same type of offence (Latimer, 1886), but not to a different type of offence (Pembliton, 1874).
10 in England and Wales (Children and Young Persons Act 1933 s 50); doli incapax presumption abolished (Crime and Disorder Act 1998 s 34; R v JTB [2009]).
Organisation liable for any offence committed by a senior manager acting within actual or apparent authority. Replaces the 2023 economic-crime rule; in force since 29 June 2026.
D is judged on the facts as D honestly believed them, even if unreasonable (Williams (Gladstone); s 76(4) CJIA 2008), unless the mistake was due to voluntary intoxication (s 76(5)).
Force is unreasonable only if grossly disproportionate; but disproportionate force must still be reasonable in all the circumstances (R (Collins) v SSJ, 2016).
D reasonably believed a threat of death or serious injury compelled the act, and a sober person of reasonable firmness sharing D's characteristics would have done the same.
Duress unavailable if D voluntarily associated with people D foresaw or ought to have foreseen might coerce D by violence; threat must be (believed) imminent.
Insanity: defect of reason from disease of the mind, so D did not know the nature and quality of the act, or did not know it was (legally) wrong.
Hypoglycaemia caused by insulin (external factor) = non-insane automatism, leading to acquittal; contrast Hennessy (hyperglycaemia, internal) = insanity.
Voluntary intoxication is no defence to basic intent crimes, but evidence of it may show that D lacked a specific intent.
Intention to kill or to cause grievous bodily harm (really serious harm): Vickers [1957]; Cunningham [1982]; DPP v Smith [1961].
Jury not entitled to find intention unless death or serious harm was virtually certain (barring unforeseen intervention) and D appreciated this.
Abnormality of mental functioning from a recognised medical condition, substantially impairing understanding, rational judgment or self-control, and explaining the killing (s 2 HA 1957).
'Substantially' impaired means important or weighty impairment, not merely more than trivial; judges should not ordinarily define it for the jury.
Fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person; or things done/said that were extremely grave and caused a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged (s 55 CJA 2009).
Sexual infidelity cannot itself be a qualifying trigger but may be considered as context where integral to other potential triggers.
Diminished responsibility: D proves on balance of probabilities. Loss of control: D raises sufficient evidence; prosecution must disprove beyond reasonable doubt.
Intentional criminal act (with its mens rea), objectively dangerous (Church), which causes death; D need not foresee harm (Newbury and Jones).
Dangerousness: the unlawful act must be one all sober and reasonable people would recognise must subject the victim to the risk of some harm.
No unlawful act where pointing a revolver in jest caused no apprehension and D did not intend an assault; mens rea of the base offence is required.
Supplier not guilty of unlawful act manslaughter where an adult freely, deliberately and with knowledge self-injected the drug.
Duty of care, breach, serious and obvious risk of death foreseeable at the time, causation, and negligence so bad it is criminal.
Risk of death must be serious and obvious on the information available at the time of breach, not on what a proper check would have revealed.

cards.f: Corporate Manslaughter and Corporate Homicide Act 2007
cards.b: Organisation liable where management of its activities causes death by gross breach of a duty of care, with senior management a substantial element.
Causing V to apprehend immediate unlawful force, intentionally or recklessly. Can be by words or silent calls (Ireland; Constanza).
Assault or battery causing hurt or injury that is more than transient or trifling; mens rea only for the assault/battery (Savage).
A break in the continuity of both layers of the skin (JCC v Eisenhower [1984]); internal bleeding alone is not a wound.
D foresaw that some physical harm might result, not necessarily serious harm (Mowatt; Parmenter).
HL: consent no defence to ABH or wounding inflicted in consensual sado-masochistic activity; public interest requires criminal sanction.
Informed consent to the risk of HIV infection may be a defence to s 20; deliberately infecting someone with intent remains s 18.
Consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is not a defence (applies to ABH and above).
Intentional penile penetration of vagina, anus or mouth; B does not consent; A does not reasonably believe B consents.
A person consents if they agree by choice and have the freedom and capacity to make that choice.
Rebuttable presumptions of no consent if A knew of e.g. violence or fear of it, unlawful detention, B asleep or unconscious, or a stupefying substance given without consent.
Deception as to the nature or purpose of the act, or impersonation of a person known personally to B: absence of consent and of reasonable belief conclusively presumed.
A drunken consent is still consent if the complainant has capacity; capacity may evaporate before unconsciousness.
Lie about a vasectomy did not negate consent under s 74: it concerned consequences, not the physical performance of the act.
Where B agreed only on the basis that A would withdraw before ejaculation, A's deliberate failure to do so meant B did not consent under s 74.
Dishonestly appropriating property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it.
HL: an act done with the owner's consent (even obtained by deception) can be an appropriation.
HL: acquiring an indefeasible title to property under a valid gift can be an appropriation; dishonesty does the work.
(1) What did D actually know or believe about the facts? (2) Was the conduct dishonest by the standards of ordinary decent people? No subjective second limb.
Not dishonest if D believes in a legal right to the property, that the owner would consent, or that the owner cannot be found by reasonable steps.
Stealing and, immediately before or at the time and in order to steal, using force on any person or putting/seeking to put them in fear of force.
Borrowing films to copy and returning them undamaged was not an intention to permanently deprive; the thing's goodness and virtue were not exhausted.
A person who aids, abets, counsels or procures an indictable offence is liable to be tried and punished as a principal.
Accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal's crime (conditional intent suffices); foresight is only evidence of intent.
If D took part in an unlawful act a reasonable person would see as risking some harm, but lacked intent for murder, D is guilty of manslaughter if death results.
Procuring means bringing about by endeavour; needs causation but no consensus, e.g. secretly spiking a driver's drink.
Usually requires timely and unequivocal communication of withdrawal to the principal(s) (Becerra and Cooper; Rook); a mere change of mind is not enough.
Communication not essential; walking away may suffice (Mitchell and King, 1999); question of fact and degree for jury (O'Flaherty, 2004).
Victim rule: a girl under the protected age could not be an accessory to an offence designed to protect her.
With intent to commit an offence, doing an act more than merely preparatory to its commission.
An act is more than merely preparatory when D has embarked on the crime proper; no need to reach the last act.
D in school toilets with rope and knife had not attempted false imprisonment: he had not actually tried to commit the offence.
Attempted murder requires an intention to kill; an intention to cause GBH is not enough.
HL: D can attempt the impossible (s 1(2)-(3) CAA 1981); overruled Anderton v Ryan using the 1966 Practice Statement.
No conspiracy where the only other party is D's spouse or civil partner, a child under 10, or the intended victim.
Doing an act capable of encouraging or assisting an offence, intending to encourage or assist its commission; complete even if no offence follows.
An offence for which no mens rea is required as to at least one element of the actus reus.
HL: presumption that mens rea is required even where the statute is silent; landlady unaware of cannabis smoking not liable.

cards.f: Gammon v AG of Hong Kong [1985]
cards.b: Presumption strong, especially for truly criminal offences; displaced only clearly or by necessary implication, for social-concern statutes where it promotes vigilance.
Presumption of mens rea applied to age; an honest (not necessarily reasonable) belief that the child was 14 or over was a defence to the old offence.
Rape of a child under 13 (s 5 SOA 2003) is strict as to age; this does not breach Article 6 ECHR.
Butcher liable for selling unfit meat although a vet had certified it fit: strict liability.
Statutory defence, e.g. Food Safety Act 1990 s 21: D not guilty if all reasonable precautions taken and all due diligence exercised.

questions.q: Which statement best captures Devlin's position in the Hart–Devlin debate?
options: Society is entitled to use the criminal law to protect its shared morality
The criminal law should only prevent harm to others
Private morality is not the law's business
Paternalism is justified but enforcing morality is not
questions.why: Devlin argued that shared morality holds society together, so society may enforce it through law. Preventing harm to others only is Mill's harm principle. 'Not the law's business' is the Wolfenden Report's view, which Devlin attacked. Accepting paternalism while rejecting enforcement of morality is Hart's reply to Devlin.

questions.q: Which case is most often used as an example of the courts enforcing morality by creating or recognising an offence, and so as a target for liberal critics?
options: Shaw v DPP [1962]
Woolmington v DPP [1935]
Sweet v Parsley [1970]
questions.why: Shaw v DPP upheld a conviction for conspiracy to corrupt public morals over a directory of prostitutes. Woolmington is about the burden of proof. R v G is about subjective recklessness. Sweet v Parsley is about the presumption of mens rea; none of those concerns enforcing morality.

questions.q: Outline the harm principle and one objection to using it as the sole limit on criminalisation. (4 marks)
markScheme: Mill (On Liberty, 1859): power may be exercised over an individual against their will only to prevent harm to others
Excludes harm to self (anti-paternalism) and mere immorality
Objection: 'harm' is indeterminate/elastic, so almost anything can be described as harmful (e.g. remote or aggregated harms)
Or: it may be too narrow (offensive conduct, Feinberg's offence principle) or say nothing about whether criminal law (rather than civil/regulatory law) is the right tool
questions.modelAnswer: The harm principle, from Mill's On Liberty (1859), says that the only legitimate reason for exercising power over someone against their will is to prevent harm to others. On this view, harm to oneself and conduct that is merely immoral are not proper grounds for criminalisation. One objection is that 'harm' is elastic: by pointing to indirect, remote or aggregated effects, almost any conduct can be described as harmful, so the principle may not limit the state much. A second is that, even where harm exists, the principle does not tell us whether the criminal law, rather than civil or regulatory law, should respond.

questions.q: D stabs V. V is taken to hospital, where a doctor negligently fails to spot a breathing problem. V dies. The stab wound is still a significant cause of death. Applying R v Cheshire, is D's act a legal cause of death?
options: Yes, because negligent treatment breaks the chain only if it is so independent and potent that D's contribution is insignificant
Yes, because D's act only needs to be a 'but for' cause
No, because any negligent medical treatment breaks the chain of causation
No, because D is only liable if the treatment was reasonable
questions.why: Cheshire holds that negligent treatment rarely breaks the chain; it must make D's act insignificant, which is not so where the wound is still a significant cause. Saying any negligence breaks the chain is the argument rejected in Cheshire. Requiring reasonable treatment reverses the test. 'But for' causation alone is not enough; legal causation is also required.

questions.q: Which case established that recklessness in English criminal law is subjective, overruling the objective test in Caldwell?
options: R v Woollin [1999]
R v Miller [1983]
R v Cunningham [1957]
questions.why: R v G overruled Caldwell. Cunningham set out a subjective test earlier but could not overrule a later House of Lords case. Woollin concerns oblique intention. Miller concerns liability for omissions after creating a danger.

questions.q: When is a person criminally liable for an omission? Give four situations with authority. (5 marks)
markScheme: No general duty to act in English law
Contractual duty (Pittwood)
Special relationship, e.g. parent and child (Gibbins and Proctor)
Voluntary assumption of care (Stone and Dobinson)
Creating a dangerous situation (Miller; Evans); statutory duties also count
questions.modelAnswer: English law has no general duty to act, so an omission is criminal only where D was under a duty. Duties arise: from contract, as in R v Pittwood (1902), where a level-crossing keeper who left the gate open was liable for manslaughter; from a special relationship such as parent and child (R v Gibbins and Proctor (1918)); from voluntarily assuming care of someone unable to look after themselves (R v Stone and Dobinson (1977)); and from creating a dangerous situation, which imposes a duty to take reasonable steps once D becomes aware of it (R v Miller (1983); R v Evans (2009)). Statutes can also impose duties.

questions.q: D, a diabetic, fails to take his insulin and, while hyperglycaemic, assaults V without awareness. Which defence is he most likely to be left with?
options: No defence, because diabetes can never affect criminal responsibility
Intoxication, because he was in an abnormal state
Insanity, because hyperglycaemia arising from the diabetes itself is an internal cause
Non-insane automatism, leading to a complete acquittal
questions.why: In R v Hennessy hyperglycaemia from not taking insulin was an internal cause, so a disease of the mind and insanity. Non-insane automatism fits hypoglycaemia caused by taking insulin, as in R v Quick, which is the opposite situation. Intoxication concerns drink or drugs, not the disease itself. Diabetes can found either insanity or automatism, so 'never' is wrong.

questions.q: D is threatened by a gang he joined knowing they used violence to enforce debts. They tell him to commit a burglary or be shot. Can he rely on duress?
options: No, because duress is never a defence to burglary
No, because he voluntarily associated with people he foresaw, or ought to have foreseen, might coerce him by violence
Yes, because a threat of death is always enough for duress
Yes, provided his belief in the threat was honest, even if unreasonable
questions.why: R v Hasan bars duress where D voluntarily joined people he foresaw or ought reasonably to have foreseen might coerce him with violence. A threat of death or serious injury is needed but is not enough on its own; the other conditions must also be met. The belief must be reasonable, not merely honest (Graham). Duress is excluded for murder and attempted murder, not burglary.

questions.q: Explain how s 76 of the Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008 governs mistaken belief and the amount of force in self-defence. (5 marks)
markScheme: Question of reasonable force judged on circumstances as D believed them (s 76(3))
Belief need only be honest; reasonableness relevant only to whether it was genuinely held (s 76(4); Williams (Gladstone))
Mistake due to voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on (s 76(5))
Force must be objectively reasonable; disproportionate force not reasonable (s 76(6)); householder: grossly disproportionate never reasonable (s 76(5A); Collins)
Retreat is a factor not a duty (s 76(6A)); heat of the moment (s 76(7))
questions.modelAnswer: Section 76 sets out the test for reasonable force. Whether the force was reasonable is decided on the circumstances as D believed them to be (s 76(3)). D's belief need only be genuine: if it was mistaken, even unreasonably, D may still rely on it, although unreasonableness is evidence that the belief was not really held (s 76(4), codifying Williams (Gladstone)). A mistake caused by voluntary intoxication cannot be relied on (s 76(5)). The force must then be reasonable on those believed facts: force that is disproportionate is not reasonable (s 76(6)), but in householder cases only grossly disproportionate force is automatically unreasonable (s 76(5A)); following Collins (2016), the jury must still decide whether force short of that was reasonable. A possibility of retreat is a factor, not a duty (s 76(6A)), and D cannot be expected to weigh the force exactly in the heat of the moment (s 76(7)).

questions.q: D sets fire to V's house at night to frighten V, knowing V is asleep upstairs. V dies. D says he did not want anyone to die. What must the jury be directed about intention?
options: Intention requires that D desired V's death
Intention is proved if D foresaw death or serious injury as probable
Intention is proved automatically if death was a virtual certainty
The jury may find intention only if death or serious injury was a virtual certainty and D appreciated that
questions.why: Woollin requires virtual certainty and D's appreciation of it, and then the jury is entitled (not obliged) to find intention. Treating foresight of a probable result as intention is the mistake corrected in Moloney and Hancock and Shankland (foresight is only evidence of intention), and Woollin then required foresight of virtual certainty. 'Automatically' ignores Matthews and Alleyne, which treats Woollin as a rule of evidence. Desire is direct intent; oblique intent covers cases where D did not want the result.

questions.q: D kills her partner after he tells her he has been unfaithful and mocks her, but the court finds nothing else was said or done. Under s 55(6)(c) of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, what is the position on loss of control?
options: The infidelity must be disregarded as a qualifying trigger, though the mockery may be considered
Loss of control is unavailable for any killing involving a partner
Infidelity can only be relied on for diminished responsibility, which is automatically available
The infidelity counts as an extremely grave circumstance
questions.why: Section 55(6)(c) requires sexual infidelity to be disregarded as a trigger, but other things said or done, such as the mockery, can still be considered; Clinton also allows infidelity as context where it is integral to them. Treating infidelity itself as an extremely grave circumstance is what the statute forbids. There is no rule excluding partners. Diminished responsibility depends on a recognised medical condition, so it is never automatic.

questions.q: Explain the three components of the loss of control defence. (5 marks)
markScheme: Loss of self-control (need not be sudden, s 54(2)); not considered desire for revenge (s 54(4))
Qualifying trigger (s 55): fear of serious violence; or extremely grave circumstances and justifiable sense of being seriously wronged; or both
Exclusions: incited triggers; sexual infidelity disregarded (Clinton qualification)
Objective test: person of D's sex and age, normal tolerance and self-restraint, in D's circumstances might have reacted similarly (s 54(1)(c))
Evidential burden on D; prosecution must disprove; partial defence reduces murder to manslaughter
questions.modelAnswer: Loss of control, under ss 54 to 56 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009, reduces murder to manslaughter. First, D must have lost self-control; it need not be sudden (s 54(2)), but the defence is unavailable if D acted in a considered desire for revenge (s 54(4)). Second, the loss of control must have a qualifying trigger (s 55): fear of serious violence from V against D or another identified person, or things done or said that amounted to circumstances of an extremely grave character and caused D to have a justifiable sense of being seriously wronged, or a combination. Incited triggers do not count and sexual infidelity is disregarded, though Clinton (2012) allows it as context. Third, a person of D's sex and age with a normal degree of tolerance and self-restraint, in D's circumstances, might have reacted in the same or a similar way. Once there is sufficient evidence, the prosecution must disprove the defence beyond reasonable doubt.

questions.q: D, a burglar, enters a house and realises during the burglary that the occupier is very old and frail. The occupier dies of a heart attack shortly after. On the dangerousness test, what is the key point?
options: Dangerousness requires a risk of serious harm
The test can never be met where the death is from a heart attack
The reasonable person is credited with the knowledge D gained during the burglary, so the risk of harm to a frail person can be recognised
The test is satisfied only if D personally foresaw a risk of harm
questions.why: R v Watson treats the sober and reasonable person as knowing what D learned during the unlawful act, including the occupier's frailty. Subjective foresight is not required (Newbury and Jones). Heart attacks are not excluded, though in Dawson the risk was not recognisable because the condition was not apparent. Church requires only a risk of some harm, not serious harm.

questions.q: A doctor fails to notice signs of a serious infection; the patient dies. Which element distinguishes gross negligence manslaughter from civil negligence?
options: That the breach caused the death
That the breach was so bad that the jury considers it criminal, and there was a serious and obvious risk of death
That the doctor intended to cause harm
That the doctor owed a duty of care
questions.why: Under Adomako the extra elements are the obvious risk of death and grossness that justifies criminal liability. A duty of care and causation are shared with civil negligence, so they do not distinguish the two. An intention to cause harm would point towards unlawful act manslaughter or murder, not negligence.

questions.q: Explain the elements of gross negligence manslaughter, with reference to Adomako and Rose. (5 marks)
markScheme: Duty of care (ordinary negligence principles)
Breach of duty
Serious and obvious risk of death, reasonably foreseeable at the time of breach (Misra; Rose: on information available to D)
Breach caused death
Negligence gross: so bad as to be criminal, for the jury (Adomako; Broughton)
questions.modelAnswer: Following Adomako (1995) and Broughton (2020), the prosecution must prove that D owed V a duty of care, assessed on ordinary negligence principles, and breached it. At the time of breach there must have been a serious and obvious risk of death, not merely of serious injury, which a reasonable person in D's position would have foreseen (Misra and Srivastava (2004)). Rose (2017) adds that this is judged on what D knew at the time; a risk that would only have been revealed by a proper examination is not enough. The breach must have caused death. Finally, the jury must find that the breach was so bad that it should be judged criminal, which is what makes the negligence 'gross'.

questions.q: D throws a stone towards V, intending only to frighten V, who sees it coming. It strikes V, causing a deep cut. D did not foresee any physical harm. Which offence, if any, is D most clearly guilty of?
options: Section 47, because D intended or was reckless as to an assault and harm was occasioned
Section 20, because a wound was caused
Section 18, because a wound was caused
No offence, because D did not intend to hit V
questions.why: D intended V to apprehend force (an assault) and the assault occasioned harm; under Savage no foresight of harm is required for s 47. Section 18 needs intent to cause GBH. Section 20 needs foresight of some physical harm (Mowatt), which D lacked. 'No offence' ignores that intending to frighten satisfies the mens rea of assault.

questions.q: Which case held that consent is no defence to injuries inflicted in consensual sado-masochistic activity in private?
options: R v Wilson [1997]
R v Dica [2004]
R v Barnes [2004]
R v Brown [1994]
questions.why: R v Brown is the House of Lords authority. Wilson allowed consent to branding by a husband at his wife's request. Barnes concerns injuries in sport. Dica concerns informed consent to the risk of HIV infection.

questions.q: Compare the mens rea for s 47, s 20 and s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. (5 marks)
markScheme: s 47: mens rea of assault/battery only (intention or subjective recklessness); no foresight of ABH needed (Savage; Roberts)
s 20: 'maliciously': intention or foresight of some physical harm (Mowatt; Parmenter), not of serious harm
s 18: specific intent to cause GBH (or resist arrest); recklessness insufficient (Belfon)
Consequence: constructive elements in s 47 and s 20, criticised for lack of correspondence
Different maximum penalties: 5 years (s 47 and s 20), life (s 18)
questions.modelAnswer: For s 47, the prosecution need only prove the mens rea of the underlying assault or battery, that is intention or subjective recklessness as to causing apprehension or applying force; D need not foresee any bodily harm (Roberts (1971); Savage (1992)). For s 20, 'maliciously' means D intended or foresaw that some physical harm might result; foresight of serious harm is unnecessary (Mowatt (1968); Parmenter (1992)). For s 18, D must intend to cause grievous bodily harm (or intend to resist arrest), and recklessness will not do (Belfon (1976)). Sections 47 and 20 therefore involve an element of constructive liability, because D can be liable for harm worse than D foresaw, which critics say breaches the correspondence principle. Section 18 carries life imprisonment; ss 47 and 20 each carry 5 years.

questions.q: A tells B he has had a vasectomy, which is untrue. B agrees to intercourse only because of this. Applying R v Lawrance [2020], is there consent under s 74?
options: No, because s 76 applies to every deception
Yes, because the lie related to the consequences of the act, not its physical performance
Yes, because consent can never be negated by deception
No, because any deception that induces intercourse negates consent
questions.why: Lawrance held that a lie about fertility does not negate consent because it is not closely connected to the physical performance of the act. 'Any deception' overstates s 74; only deceptions closely connected to the act do (e.g. condom use in Assange). Section 76 covers only deception as to nature or purpose, or impersonation of a person known personally. 'Never' ignores s 76 and cases like McNally under s 74.

questions.q: Which of these circumstances triggers a conclusive (irrebuttable) presumption of no consent under the Sexual Offences Act 2003?
options: B had been given a stupefying drug without consent
B was asleep at the time
A induced B's consent by impersonating B's partner
A used violence against B immediately before the act
questions.why: Impersonating someone known personally to B is one of the two s 76 conclusive presumptions. Sleep, violence and a stupefying substance are s 75 circumstances, which create only evidential (rebuttable) presumptions.

questions.q: Explain how the Sexual Offences Act 2003 deals with a defendant's belief in consent in rape. (4 marks)
markScheme: Mens rea: A does not reasonably believe B consents (s 1(1)(c))
Reasonableness decided having regard to all circumstances, including steps taken to ascertain consent (s 1(2))
s 75: evidential presumption that A did not reasonably believe in consent if listed circumstances known to A, unless sufficient evidence raised
s 76: conclusive presumption of no reasonable belief where deception as to nature/purpose or impersonation
questions.modelAnswer: Under s 1(1)(c) A is guilty of rape only if A does not reasonably believe that B consents, so an honest but unreasonable belief is no defence. Under s 1(2), whether a belief is reasonable is judged having regard to all the circumstances, including any steps A took to find out whether B consented. Where a s 75 circumstance exists and A knew of it (for example, B was asleep), A is presumed not to have reasonably believed in consent unless sufficient evidence is raised to the contrary. Where s 76 applies (deception as to the nature or purpose of the act, or impersonation of a person known personally to B), it is conclusively presumed both that B did not consent and that A did not reasonably believe that B consented.

questions.q: D takes £50 from a colleague's drawer, honestly believing the colleague owes him that sum and he is legally entitled to it. Is D guilty of theft?
options: Yes, because a belief must be reasonable to negate dishonesty
No, because money is not property under s 4
No, because under s 2(1)(a) D is not dishonest if he believes he has a legal right to the property
Yes, because ordinary decent people would consider taking money from a drawer dishonest
questions.why: Section 2(1)(a) deems D not dishonest if he believes he has a legal right, so the Ivey test is never reached. Going straight to the standards of ordinary decent people skips s 2. The belief need only be genuine, not reasonable (though unreasonableness is evidence it was not held). Money is property under s 4.

questions.q: Under Ivey v Genting and R v Barton and Booth, which statement about dishonesty is correct?
options: The jury must ask whether D realised ordinary decent people would regard the conduct as dishonest
Dishonesty is a question of law for the judge
Dishonesty depends only on D's own standards of honesty
The jury first establishes D's actual knowledge or belief about the facts, then applies the standards of ordinary decent people
questions.why: Ivey, confirmed in Barton and Booth, removed Ghosh's second, subjective limb. Asking whether D realised others would see it as dishonest is that abolished Ghosh limb. D's own standards are irrelevant; only D's beliefs about the facts count. Dishonesty is a question of fact for the jury.

questions.q: D is allowed into a department store, then goes into a staff-only stockroom intending to steal. Explain whether D commits burglary. (5 marks)
markScheme: s 9(1)(a): entry as trespasser into building or part of building with intent to steal
Permission to enter shop does not extend to staff-only areas; exceeding permission = trespasser (Jones and Smith)
Stockroom is a 'part of a building' (Walkington, counter area)
D must know or be reckless that he is trespassing (Collins)
Intent to steal at time of entry into the part: conditional intent suffices; conclusion: burglary
questions.modelAnswer: Burglary under s 9(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968 requires entry into a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to steal. D had permission to be in the public part of the store, but that permission did not extend to the stockroom; entering an area beyond one's permission makes one a trespasser (Jones and Smith (1976)). A staff-only area is a 'part of a building', as the counter area was in Walkington (1979). D must know, or be reckless as to whether, he is trespassing (Collins (1973)), which is likely given the 'staff only' sign. D intended to steal when he entered that part. So D commits burglary as soon as he enters the stockroom, even before taking anything.

questions.q: A and B agree to rob a shop. B knows A has a knife and agrees that A should use it to cause serious injury if anyone resists, though B hopes it will not be needed. A stabs and kills the shopkeeper with intent to kill. Under Jogee, what is B's liability?
options: Guilty of murder only because B foresaw that A might use the knife
Guilty of murder, because B had a conditional intention to assist A to cause serious harm if necessary
Guilty of manslaughter only, because B did not personally use force
Not guilty of murder, because B did not want anyone to be hurt
questions.why: Jogee confirms that conditional intent counts: B intended to assist serious violence if needed, which is enough for murder. Desire is not required, so B's hope that it would not be needed does not help. Foresight alone was the Chan Wing-Siu rule that Jogee rejected; it is now only evidence. Manslaughter is the route where the accessory lacks intent to assist serious harm, which is not this case.

questions.q: C agrees with D to attack V at a planned time. An hour before, C decides not to go and stays at home without telling D. D attacks V. Has C effectively withdrawn?
options: Yes, because C was not present at the scene
Yes, because a change of mind is enough
No, because withdrawal is never possible once a plan is made
No, because in a planned attack withdrawal usually requires timely and unequivocal communication to the others
questions.why: Becerra and Rook require more than staying away: in planned crimes withdrawal usually has to be communicated (in Rook the defendant who simply did not turn up remained liable). Absence from the scene does not cancel earlier encouragement or assistance. A change of mind alone is not enough. Withdrawal is possible if done properly, so 'never' is wrong.

questions.q: Explain the mental element required for secondary liability after R v Jogee [2016]. (5 marks)
markScheme: Intention to assist or encourage the principal to commit the crime
Knowledge of existing facts necessary for the principal's conduct to be criminal
Conditional intent suffices; desire not necessary
Foresight is evidence of intent, not a substitute (Chan Wing-Siu/Powell and English overruled)
Murder/manslaughter: accessory lacking intent for murder may be guilty of manslaughter where reasonable person would recognise risk of some harm
questions.modelAnswer: In Jogee (2016) the Supreme Court held that an accessory must intend to assist or encourage the principal to commit the crime. Where the principal's conduct is criminal only in particular circumstances, the accessory must know of those existing facts. Intention to assist is different from wanting the crime to happen, and a conditional intention, for example to assist violence if it becomes necessary, is enough. The court overruled the Chan Wing-Siu approach under which foresight that the principal might commit the crime was sufficient; foresight is now only evidence from which intent may be inferred. If the principal kills and the accessory lacked an intent to assist killing or serious harm, the accessory may still be guilty of manslaughter if they took part in an unlawful act that a reasonable person would see as carrying a risk of some harm.
