questions.q: D buys a balaclava and an imitation gun and walks towards a post office intending to rob it, but is arrested just outside before entering. Following R v Campbell, what is the likely outcome on a charge of attempted robbery?
options: Guilty, because D had formed a firm intention and was close to the post office
Not guilty, because robbery cannot be attempted
Guilty, because buying the gun was more than merely preparatory
Not guilty, because D had not yet gone beyond preparation by entering or confronting anyone
questions.why: In Campbell the defendant was close to the post office but had not entered, so his acts were merely preparatory. Intention plus closeness is not enough; the test is whether D has embarked on the crime proper (Gullefer). Buying equipment is classic preparation. Robbery is an indictable offence and can be attempted.

questions.q: D is caught selling a substance he believes to be heroin. It is in fact harmless powder. Is he guilty of attempting to supply a controlled drug?
options: Yes, because under s 1(2)–(3) Criminal Attempts Act 1981 he is judged on the facts as he believed them (R v Shivpuri)
No, because Anderton v Ryan holds that objectively innocent acts cannot be attempts
Yes, but only if a reasonable person would also have believed it was heroin
No, because it was impossible to commit the full offence
questions.why: Shivpuri applies s 1(2)–(3): impossibility is no bar and D is judged on his belief. Saying impossibility prevents liability is the position the 1981 Act reversed. Anderton v Ryan was overruled by Shivpuri. There is no requirement that a reasonable person would share D's belief.

questions.q: How do the courts decide whether an act is 'more than merely preparatory'? Refer to three cases. (5 marks)
markScheme: Question of fact for jury once judge decides there is evidence (s 4(3))
Gullefer: D must have embarked on the crime proper; no need for last act
Jones: pointing gun at V in car = attempt even with safety catch on
Campbell: outside post office, not entered = merely preparatory
Geddes: had D actually tried to commit the offence? (school toilets; not attempt); Tosti contrasted
questions.modelAnswer: Under s 1(1) of the Criminal Attempts Act 1981, D must do an act that is more than merely preparatory; the judge decides whether there is evidence on which a jury could so find, and the jury decides the question. In Gullefer (1990) the Court of Appeal said D must have embarked on the 'crime proper', though D need not have reached the last act. In Jones (1990), getting into V's car and pointing a loaded gun at him was an attempt even though the safety catch was on. By contrast, in Campbell (1991) a man with an imitation gun just outside a post office had not attempted robbery, and in Geddes (1996) a man in school toilets with rope and a knife had not attempted false imprisonment because he had not actually tried to commit it. In Tosti (1997), examining a padlock with cutting equipment nearby was an attempt.

questions.q: In Gammon v Attorney-General of Hong Kong, Lord Scarman said the presumption of mens rea can be displaced only where the statute is concerned with what?
options: Offences against the person
Offences committed only by companies
Any offence with a maximum penalty below two years
An issue of social concern, such as public safety, where strict liability will encourage greater vigilance
questions.why: Gammon limits strict liability to social-concern statutes where it promotes the statute's object. Low penalty is relevant but is not the test. Offences against the person are 'truly criminal', where the presumption is strongest. Strict liability is not confined to companies; individuals were liable in Callow v Tillstone.

questions.q: D, aged 18, has intercourse with a 12-year-old who told him she was 15 and looked older. Charged under s 5 of the Sexual Offences Act 2003, can he rely on his belief about her age?
options: No, because s 5 is strict as to age, as confirmed in R v G [2008]
No, because the presumption of mens rea never applies to sexual offences
Yes, because B v DPP requires an honest belief about age to be a defence
Yes, if his belief was reasonable
questions.why: R v G held that s 5 imposes strict liability as to age and that this is compatible with Article 6. B v DPP concerned an older offence where the statute did not displace the presumption; s 5 clearly does. Reasonableness of belief is irrelevant under s 5. The presumption does apply to sexual offences generally (B v DPP itself was one), so 'never' is wrong.

questions.q: Give two arguments for and two against strict liability in criminal law. (4 marks)
markScheme: For: protects public in areas of social concern (Gammon)
For: encourages vigilance; eases enforcement where fault hard to prove
Against: punishes the blameless; conflicts with fault principle
Against: doubtful deterrent effect; stigma and penalties can be serious (R v G); due diligence defences as compromise
questions.modelAnswer: In favour: strict liability protects the public in areas of social concern such as food safety and pollution, which is why Gammon allows it there; and it encourages businesses to take high standards of care while making enforcement practical, because proving the mens rea of busy traders or companies is difficult. Against: it punishes people who are not at fault, breaking the principle that criminal liability should follow blame; and it is doubtful that it improves standards more than fault-based offences, while some strict offences carry serious stigma and penalties, as in R v G. A due diligence defence is a common compromise.

questions.q: Problem question. Asha and Ben, who are both 19, decide to break into Carl's flat to steal his games console. Asha knows that Ben sometimes carries a knife, and before they set out she tells him, 'Only use it if he wakes up and won't let us go.' On the way there, Dev, who had agreed to keep watch, says 'I'm not doing this, it's stupid', and goes home. Inside the flat, Carl wakes up and grabs Asha's arm. Ben stabs Carl in the chest, intending to kill him. Carl dies. Discuss the criminal liability of Asha, Ben and Dev. (25 marks)
markScheme: Ben: burglary (s 9(1)(a) Theft Act 1968 entry as trespasser with intent to steal), aggravated as he had a knife on entry (s 10); murder: unlawful killing, causation, intent to kill; no partial defence on facts
Asha: burglary as joint principal; secondary liability for murder under Accessories and Abettors Act 1861 s 8
Asha's mental element post-Jogee: conditional intent to assist use of knife if Carl resisted; intention to assist serious harm suffices for murder; foresight only evidence
If jury finds she did not intend serious harm: manslaughter route (unlawful act a reasonable person would see as risking some harm)
Overwhelming supervening act not applicable: knife use was within what she contemplated
Dev: secondary liability for burglary (and possibly homicide) via agreement/encouragement; conspiracy to burgle (Criminal Law Act 1977 s 1) complete on agreement
Dev's withdrawal: planned crime; he did communicate unequivocally and in time (Becerra; Rook; contrast Mitchell and King); likely effective for secondary liability but conspiracy already complete
Structured conclusions with reasons
questions.modelAnswer:
Ben

Ben entered Carl's flat as a trespasser with intent to steal, so he commits burglary under s 9(1)(a) of the Theft Act 1968. On entry with that intention the offence is complete, and because he had a knife with him when he entered, it is aggravated burglary (s 10). He is also guilty of murder: he caused Carl's death by stabbing him, there is no break in the chain of causation, and he intended to kill, which is malice aforethought. Nothing suggests a qualifying trigger for loss of control (Carl grabbing Asha's arm is unlikely to be fear of serious violence or an extremely grave circumstance), and there is no evidence of a recognised medical condition for diminished responsibility.

Asha

Asha is a joint principal in the burglary. Her liability for murder is secondary under s 8 of the Accessories and Abettors Act 1861. The conduct element is met: she took part in the burglary with Ben and her words before they set out encouraged him to use the knife in a particular event.

The mental element is governed by Jogee (2016). She must have intended to assist or encourage Ben to commit the crime, with knowledge of the essential facts. Foresight that Ben might use the knife is not enough in itself; it is only evidence of intention. But Jogee expressly accepts conditional intent: an accessory who agrees that violence will be used if necessary intends to assist that violence. Her instruction, 'Only use it if he wakes up and won't let us go', is strong evidence that she intended to encourage the use of the knife to cause at least serious harm if Carl resisted. Stabbing someone in the chest is the kind of use she contemplated, so there is no overwhelming supervening act. If the jury find that she intended to assist the intentional infliction of serious harm or death, she is guilty of murder.

If the jury are not sure of that (for example, if they think she meant only that Ben should threaten Carl with the knife), she is not guilty of murder. However, under Jogee she would be guilty of manslaughter, because she took part in an unlawful act (burglary while armed) that any reasonable person would realise carried a risk of some harm, and death resulted.

Dev

Dev agreed to keep watch, so by agreeing with Asha and Ben to commit burglary he is guilty of statutory conspiracy under s 1 of the Criminal Law Act 1977. Conspiracy is complete on agreement, so his later change of mind does not affect it.

For secondary liability for the burglary and the homicide, the question is withdrawal. This was a planned crime, so withdrawal usually requires timely and unequivocal communication (Becerra and Cooper (1975); Rook (1993)). Unlike the defendant in Rook, who simply failed to turn up, Dev told the others clearly that he was not going ahead, before they reached the flat. He gave no material help (his promise to keep watch had not been acted on), so his communication is probably enough to neutralise his earlier encouragement. He is therefore probably not liable as an accessory to the burglary or to murder or manslaughter, but remains guilty of conspiracy to burgle.

questions.q: Essay. 'The law on consent to bodily harm, from R v Brown to the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, is incoherent and unjustifiably paternalistic.' Discuss. (25 marks)
markScheme: Explains general rule: consent no defence where ABH or more intended/caused unless exception (AG's Ref No 6 of 1980; Brown)
Brown: majority reasoning (public interest, risk of harm, corruption) and dissent (privacy, Lord Mustill's analysis)
Exceptions: sport (Barnes), surgery, tattooing, horseplay, Wilson (branding) vs Emmett and BM; Dica/Konzani informed consent to risk
Incoherence: line between Wilson and Brown; inconsistent treatment of risk vs intended harm; sexual vs non-sexual contexts
Paternalism critique: Mill's harm principle and Hart's distinction; autonomy; ECHR Art 8 (Laskey, Jaggard and Brown v UK 1997 found no violation)
Defence of the law: public interest, protection of vulnerable people, difficulty of proving genuine consent in domestic abuse; s 71 DAA 2021 'rough sex' defence response
Reform: Law Commission work (Consent in the Criminal Law, 1995) and options
Reasoned conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The starting point is that consent is a defence to common assault and battery, but generally not where actual bodily harm or worse is intended or caused, unless the activity falls within a recognised exception (Attorney-General's Reference (No 6 of 1980); R v Brown (1994)). The question is whether this structure is coherent and whether its limits on autonomy can be justified.

In Brown the House of Lords, by a 3–2 majority, upheld convictions under ss 47 and 20 for consensual sado-masochistic injuries in private. The majority stressed the public interest, the risk of infection and serious injury, and the danger of corrupting young men. Lords Mustill and Slynn dissented, arguing that the activities were private and that the Offences Against the Person Act was not designed for them. The European Court of Human Rights later found no violation of Article 8 (Laskey, Jaggard and Brown v UK (1997)), because states have a margin of appreciation in protecting health.

The charge of incoherence is strong. The recognised exceptions (sport, surgery, tattooing, rough horseplay) rest on social approval rather than a clear principle. In Wilson (1997) a husband who branded his initials on his wife's buttocks at her request was not guilty, the court treating it as like tattooing and a private matter between spouses; yet in Emmett (1999) consent was no defence to harm in sexual activity between partners, and in BM (2018) body modification by a tattooist was not an exception. In Dica (2004) and Konzani (2005), informed consent to the risk of HIV infection is a defence to s 20, which sits oddly with Brown's refusal to allow consent to intended, lesser harm. The law seems to depend on judges' views of the activity's social value.

On paternalism, a Millian liberal would say harm to consenting adults is not the state's business. Hart accepted some paternalism, for example to protect people whose consent may not be genuine. That is the strongest justification of the current law: in domestic settings, apparent consent can mask coercion, and the 'rough sex' defence was raised in several high-profile killings of women. Section 71 of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 put the Brown principle on a statutory footing by providing that consent to serious harm for sexual gratification is no defence. This responds to a real social problem, but it does not resolve the broader incoherence.

A better approach might start from autonomy, with clearer limits based on the seriousness of harm (for example, allowing consent up to a fixed level of injury), safeguards on capacity and genuine consent, and a statutory list of exceptions. The Law Commission explored such options in Consent in the Criminal Law (Consultation Paper No 139, 1995), but no general reform followed.

In conclusion, the law is incoherent in how it draws its exceptions, and Brown's reasoning relies on moral disapproval as much as on harm. However, it is not wholly unjustified: protecting people from coercion disguised as consent is a legitimate aim, as s 71 shows. The case for reform lies in replacing case-by-case social judgments with a principled statutory scheme.
